guides.title: Write your first great image prompt
guides.summary: Build a prompt in six layers — subject, style, light, camera, mood, format — and change one layer at a time.

steps.title: Say what's in the picture
steps.body: Start with one plain sentence: who or what, doing what, where. Concrete nouns beat adjectives — "an elderly ceramicist holding a half-finished vase" gives the model far more to work with than "a beautiful artistic portrait".

steps.title: Name the medium
steps.body: Is it a photo, an oil painting, a 3D render, a flat vector? One or two words up front set everything else. A publication or genre ("editorial portrait", "catalog photography") works as shorthand for a whole look.

steps.title: Describe the light
steps.body: Light does most of the emotional work. Say where it comes from and what it does: "soft window light from the left", "a sharp circle of afternoon sun". Time of day (golden hour, blue hour) is a quick way in.

steps.title: Place the camera
steps.body: Angle and lens decide what the viewer feels. "Overhead flat-lay", "low angle", "85mm at f/1.8" (blurry background), "wide-angle" (more space, more drama). Photo terms work even for illustrations.

steps.title: Set colour and mood
steps.body: Pick a small palette — two or three colours — or a mood word. "Muted greens and gold" keeps an image coherent; "vibrant" on its own usually just means oversaturated.

steps.title: Fix the format, then iterate
steps.body: State the aspect ratio ("4:5 vertical", "wide 16:9"). Generate, then change one layer at a time so you learn what each phrase does. Open any prompt in the gallery and turn on Highlight anatomy to see these layers in real prompts.

guides.title: Turn a phone photo of a product into a catalog shot
guides.summary: Use an image-editing model to restage a real product on a studio set without changing the product itself.

steps.title: Take a clean source photo
steps.body: Shoot the product in daylight against a plain background, filling most of the frame. The model can only keep detail it can see — logos, stitching and texture should be sharp.

steps.title: Upload it and lock what must not change
steps.body: Start your prompt with what stays: "Keep the product exactly as in the photo — shape, colour, logo and proportions." Editing models follow the first instruction most faithfully.

steps.title: Describe the new set
steps.body: Then describe the scene: the surface (travertine plinth, linen, wet slate), the backdrop colour, and the light. Echo the product's colours in the backdrop so the image reads as one palette.

steps.title: Generate several, keep the best
steps.body: Ask for three or four versions. Compare them at full size — small text and logos are where models most often slip.

steps.title: Fix details with a follow-up
steps.body: Instead of starting over, reply with one change: "same image, softer shadow", "move the camera lower". The same "say what stays first" rule works for rooms and spaces too.

guides.title: Design a game character, from idea to turnaround
guides.summary: Go from a one-line idea to a front, side and back reference sheet you can reuse for poses or 3D.

steps.title: Write the character in one sentence
steps.body: Combine a familiar thing with an unexpected one: "a friendly robot shaped like a teapot". If the sentence is memorable, the design usually is too.

steps.title: Choose a style you can repeat
steps.body: Flat vector with thick outlines, cel-shaded anime, or painted — pick one and keep the same words in every later prompt. A limited palette (three named colours) makes the character recognisable.

steps.title: Ask for a character sheet
steps.body: Use the words "character sheet" and name the views: "three views (front, side, back), white background". You get a turnaround in one image.

steps.title: Reuse the sheet as a reference
steps.body: Upload the sheet with your next prompt ("this character, waving, sitting on a shelf") to keep it consistent. In Midjourney, character reference (--cref) does the same job.

steps.title: Take it further
steps.body: The turnaround is exactly what a 3D modeller — or a text-to-3D tool — needs. Check the Game dev category in Repos for tools that connect AI assistants to engines like Blender, Unity and Godot.

guides.title: Make a poster with text that's actually readable
guides.summary: Models now render lettering well — if you quote the words, describe the type, and keep it short.

steps.title: Choose a model that handles type
steps.body: Ideogram, FLUX and GPT Image are the strongest at lettering. Older Stable Diffusion models usually garble text; if you're using one, ask for no text and add it in an editor.

steps.title: Quote the exact words
steps.body: Put the text in quotes and say where it sits: the label reads "NORTHBOUND ROASTERS" in a condensed serif, with smaller text underneath.

steps.title: Describe the lettering, not just the font
steps.body: "Hand-lettered script", "bold condensed sans", "small caps" — models understand type styles better than font names.

steps.title: Keep it short
steps.body: One headline and one small line is reliable. Paragraphs of body text are not — leave those for your design tool.

steps.title: Or ask for no text at all
steps.body: For illustration-led posters, "no text" stops the model inventing fake lettering, and leaves you clean space to set your own.

guides.title: Give your AI assistant design skills
guides.summary: Skills are folders of instructions an AI agent loads when a task calls for them. Here's how to find and use them.

steps.title: Know what a skill is
steps.body: A skill is a folder with a short instruction file (and sometimes scripts or examples) that teaches an agent how to do one kind of task well — making slides, following a brand, reviewing a design. The agent reads it only when it's relevant.

steps.title: Start with the official set
steps.body: Anthropic publishes a collection of example skills covering documents, design and more. Read a couple of their instruction files — they're plain text and show what good guidance looks like.

steps.title: Browse by the work you do
steps.body: Open Repos and pick the Design category, then set Kind to Skill. Sort by Rising to see what other people are adopting this week.

steps.title: Install it the way the repo says
steps.body: Each repo's README explains how to install it for your tool — usually copying a folder into your project or adding a plugin. Follow that rather than guessing; tools differ.

steps.title: Ask for it by name, then review
steps.body: Mention the skill in your request ("use the design-review skill on this page"). Check the result yourself: a skill makes the agent more consistent, not infallible.

steps.title: Borrow from design systems
steps.body: Collections of design-system notes can be dropped into a project so the agent matches a brand's look.
